entry.title: The Post-Quantum Future of Web Privacy
entry.content:
The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.

Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.

With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.

Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology  can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.

This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.

But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.

What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE

Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.

One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.

One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.

Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.

However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.

This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.

An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.

Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.

A feast of cryptography

When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.

Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.

Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.

We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.

This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.

VOLE-in-the-Head

The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y  are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.

Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.

One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).

Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.

The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.

When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.

Multivariate signatures

Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.

The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.

UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures.

The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough.

Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOV

Earlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published (Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often.

This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions. But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail.

A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment. For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly.

To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof.

Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer:

  1. The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer.
  2. The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash.
  3. Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1,

The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m.

Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions.

The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.)

Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) where s is the signature, rs is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting.

From blind signatures to endorsements and beyond

Recall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P1,…,PN, and the statement we now want to prove is  Pi(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) for some anchor key Pi whose index i is now part of the hidden witness.

With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter.

Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH.

Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board.

Optimizations

Before we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions.

On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve.

Using fewer hashes

PoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.

This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.

This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.

In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.

Making each hash cheaper

Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.

Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.

Leaning into multivariate

In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.

This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.

We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.

Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).

For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.

There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.

And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.

Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?

We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.

Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:

issuance

presentation

PoMFRIT (with UOV)

<1KB

4.3KB (redemption)

VOLE-IHAT

5.6KB

6.5KB (redemption)

VOLE-ACT

5.4KB

12.0KB (spend)


These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)

If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.

We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

The post-quantum future of web privacyhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/vole-mole/

entry.title: Octoverse: Commits, Pushes, Reach New Highs in 2026 as Developers Build With Agents
entry.content:
Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined.

Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati, a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft, and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers. Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before.

That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture.

Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most:

  • More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one.
  • As of September, developers start more than 40% of pull requests with an agent. In March, it was 17%. For a growing share of work, the first move is now directing an agent, and review is how developers shape what comes back.
  • Developers move fast on model choice. In September, 61% of GitHub Copilot users used more than one model, and requests spread across general purpose, deep reasoning and planning, and fast and lightweight models
  • Builders are showing up from every field. This year, for the first time, we’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry. Repos serving mining, construction, health care, and agriculture have each grown several times over since 2022.

Underneath it all, AI models and the harnesses built around them have advanced over the past year, and developers have more to choose from. Growth is moving quickly: one year into last year’s five-year developer growth projections, every country we projected has already closed at least a fifth of its distance to 2030, and our own forecasting models no longer agree on where it will go next.

The year developers set a new pace

This year was all about momentum. Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day.

Agents were one of the tools developers leaned on hardest this year, pulling them deeper into daily work. Among repos created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one, sign that individuals and teams building with agents from day one are moving at a markedly different pace.

Developers also relied on automations to keep projects moving. GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year. This equals 124 million times a day and is more than three times last year’s total. Developers merged more than 30 million Dependabot pull requests to keep dependencies current and reduce the use of known vulnerabilities, about double 2025’s pace.

Our telemetry shows activity climbing steadily from January, then surging around June, as if developers everywhere saw new possibilities at once. Right around then, a cluster of industry-wide shifts landed: better underlying models, the harnesses and tools built around them, and the agents running on both. Agents moved from single-session tools to persistent ones that could track progress across days and orchestrate other specialized agents. Just as important, agents began making extensive use of the cloud, executing work remotely as well as on local machines.

This momentum is showing up both in brand-new repos and from developers who have been building for years. From June onwards, about 55% of all commits came from brand new repositories. But plenty more commits came from developers who’ve been around a while: developers who pushed code in the past 12 months have been on GitHub for an average of 36 months, and of those who opened a pull request in August, more than 75% pushed code in September. They are also branching out: the average developer now works across 10% more repositories than they did a year ago.

That staying power shows up in open source too. Public contributions soared to 2.5 billion in 2026, more than double last year’s total (1.12 billion). Behind those numbers are developers who keep showing up, like @kinlane, who made more than 1 million contributions across his public repositories using agentic workflows to keep a machine-readable catalog of public API information current. Another example is @kim-em, who made more than 178,000 contributions while maintaining mathlib, which is a community library of computer-checked mathematics. @andig, a maintainer of the open source EV charging controller and home energy management system evcc, contributed over 21,000 times.

These are just a few examples of the work millions of developers do every day. To all the developers doing work like this and beyond: we see you, and we’re glad you’re building.

Developers are building from more places

Behind every number in this report is a developer. GitHub now serves more than 225 million of them, and the community is growing around the globe. The United States (38.3 million) and India (32 million) remain the two largest developer communities, and each added more than 10 million developers this year. Brazil added 3.28 million developers on GitHub this year, the third most of any country.

Last year, we projected that India would reach 57.5 million developers by 2030 and the United States 54.7 million. One year into that five-year window, every country in our projections has already closed at least a fifth of the distance to its own 2030 figure. The United States has closed 38.6%, and India 28.3%.

The same momentum shows up across regions, each with its own local context:

One year in, growth is strong against last year’s projection, and projecting the next five years is getting harder. We ran more than 40 forecasting models forward to 2031, time-series and regression models built on historical sign-up and usage data, each assuming a different pace of growth. About half call for “extreme” growth, with developer counts on GitHub more than tripling by 2031. Just under half call for “substantial” growth, doubling to tripling. Only three models expect anything close to modest, under 2x growth.

Forecasts are estimates, and a spread this wide shows how much the 2026 surge widened what is plausible by 2031. What holds steady is the shape of the trend: a developer community growing in more places at once.

The future is being built everywhere

In past reports, “everywhere” meant more developers and more countries, such as in the context of the top countries contributing code to public repositories:

Top 10 countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location 

This year, it also means more fields, including industries we haven’t measured before.

We’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), which sorts economic activity into sectors. A language model classified random samples of public repositories created each year from 2022 to 2026, assigning each to the industry it serves based on its name, description, topics, and README. We also tracked two signals: whether a repository mentions AI, and whether an agent opened a pull request against it.

The two signals do not always move together. In administrative and support services, mining, health care, and agriculture, more than four in 10 repositories mention AI, yet agent-opened pull requests are rare, less than 3 percent. Construction breaks that pattern. About a quarter of its repositories mention AI, but about 9 percent have agent-opened pull requests, the highest share of any sector, with manufacturing next.

The same classification shows how each industry’s footprint has shifted since 2022, and sectors well beyond software are climbing. Professional, scientific, and technical services rose from fourth to second place among all industries, behind only information. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting climbed two spots, and finance and insurance and health care and social assistance each moved up one. Against each sector’s own 2022 baseline, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction grew roughly 65 times from a small starting base, administrative and support services and construction 17 to 18 times, and even manufacturing, the slowest of these, almost tripled.

Behind these sector shifts are people who know their fields, now using AI coding agents to build. For example, in manufacturing, a small team built a way to turn a photo of your tools into a custom-fit, 3D-printable drawer organizer. A research lab in health care made it easier for scientists to analyze huge digital scans of tissue samples, the kind pathologists study to understand disease. In Copenhagen, a university lab built a pipeline that classifies video of chickens at play, from frolicking to worm chasing. A University of Waikato energy center built a toolkit that helps industrial plants find heat they can reuse, and Bulgaria’s digital ministry open-sourced a portal where anyone can trace who won a public contract and for how much. For writers, a novelist built a free app that makes a manuscript look like a book as you type. In field after field, the people closest to the problem are building the solution, with agents helping along the way.

Professional, scientific, and technical services, which grew about 5 times over its own 2022 baseline and climbed to second place, is the work of researching, engineering, and advising, and open code has long been part of how that work gets done. In biochemistry, the work behind AlphaFold earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In computer science, Tensor2Tensor accompanied the paper that introduced the Transformer, the architecture behind today’s large language models, “Attention Is All You Need.” In medicine, sars-cov-2-stability held the code and data behind one of the earliest papers on how long the virus survives in the air and on surfaces. In physics, eht-imaging was one of two open-source libraries used to reconstruct the first image of a black hole. A repository has quietly become part of the paper trail behind published research.

Developers are reshaping their workflow

More developers now begin a pull request by specifying what they want and orchestrating the agents that carry it out. By September 2026, more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March. That is 110 million in September alone, about 6x March’s volume.

Agent-started pull requests also more often change multiple files: about 87%, compared with 79% of pull requests without detected agent involvement. They are landing quickly too. In February, 83% of agent-involved pull requests merged within two weeks, a touch behind the roughly 86% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. By September, agent pull requests were at 90%, while the comparison group held at about 86%.

Among GitHub Copilot’s monthly active users, 55% now use agentic features, up from 35% a year ago. The steepest growth is in the most hands-off mode. Copilot cloud agent, where a developer assigns a task and an agent works on it independently, grew 230% year over year, against 85% for agent chat. Developers still ask agents questions, and increasingly they hand over whole tasks.

The willingness to delegate is reflected by the kinds of tasks developers are attempting. Public repositories mentioning interoperability or reverse engineering increased more than 300% year over year, from about 30,000 created in 2025 to more than 130,000 in 2026.

Review is where developers shape what comes back, and more tooling is being built for it. Stacked pull requests, which split related work into smaller changes that are easier to review in sequence, launched as a preview on July 30, and more than 264,000 developers had used them by September. Usage of AI-assisted code review and GitHub Advanced Security both grew more than 90% year over year. The platform also helps secure that work: push protection, which screens for exposed secrets such as API keys and passwords, ran 5.8 billion scans this year, nearly four times 2025’s pace. Developers are investing in how they review code.

Model choice moves at developer speed

Developers match models to the work they hand to their agents. In September 2026, 61% of GitHub Copilot users who selected a model themselves used more than one model across their sessions, up from 50% four months earlier.

The lineup is growing too: developers on paid GitHub Copilot plans used 29 distinct models in May and 47 in September, and no single model carried more than 25% of requests that month. Some model decisions come down to cost and familiarity. Developers weigh price and functionality against need and may lean toward providers they already trust.

To see how developer choices spread, we grouped the models used in GitHub Copilot by what they are built for: deep reasoning and planning, general purpose, and fast and lightweight. We then looked at where requests went, counting only activity where a developer explicitly selected a model. That leaves out cases where GitHub Copilot picks the model (auto model selection), GitHub and Microsoft staff usage, background utility models, duplicate requests used for monitoring and testing, and requests made with a developer’s own API key.

We found that out of every 100 developer-selected requests, 38 went to general purpose models, 37 to deep reasoning and planning models, and 25 to fast and lightweight models. Developers spread their choices across models and functionality, and about 25% of requests go to a fast model.

To see how those choices shift, we looked at them as a time series over the past three months, tracking request share alongside how many developers tried each model and how many kept coming back. Three patterns stand out:

  • New releases are used heavily before most developers have tried them. In their first weeks, most new models take a larger share of requests than the portion of developers who have tried them. Early adopters use a model heavily before the rest follow.
  • Developers keep a model in rotation after leaning on it less. When a model’s share of requests falls, the share of developers still using it falls more slowly
  • Developers blend kinds of models. Requests spread across all three groups, and few developers stay with any one kind for long.

Taken together, the spread across kinds of models points to a lot of choosing: a lineup that keeps growing, a best fit that shifts from one task to the next, and all three kinds of models held in rotation. Many developers also let GitHub Copilot do some of it. In September 2026, 63% of paying GitHub Copilot developers used auto model selection at least once, letting Copilot pick the model for the task.

Planning, implementing, and checking a change each place different demands on a model, in capability, speed, and cost. Project HydraFusion, began as a research preview of model orchestration, matching models to each step of that work. In the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, it routed almost 60,000 sessions. That work is now generally available as GitHub Copilot Fusion, which brings model orchestration together with auto model selection and chooses the right model for each step behind the scenes.

Language choice has new influence

Language choice has long reflected what developers want to build, what their teams know, and what existing systems require. This year’s data raises the question of whether a fourth influence is emerging: the language an agent picks when a developer doesn’t specify one.

Last year, we reported that TypeScript had overtaken Python and JavaScript to become the most used language on GitHub by contributors. That order held in 2026, with TypeScript first, Python second, and JavaScript third. The pace picked up. From September 2025 to September 2026, TypeScript added 3.62 million monthly contributors, Python 3.23 million, and JavaScript 1.82 million, the largest gains among the top 10 languages. Rust grew fastest by percentage among the top languages, doubling in the past year.

Our forecasts extend recent trends: TypeScript and Python near 13 million monthly contributors each by September 2027, JavaScript at 7.4 million, and every other language in the top 10 below about 2.2 million.

The languages growing fastest are also where AI shows up most. We charted each language’s community growth over the past year against the share of its merged pull requests with detected AI involvement, with bubbles roughly sized to show the size of each language’s community. TypeScript, Python, and Rust, the fastest-growing communities, have the highest shares, about 40% to 44% of merged pull requests. Java, C#, and C++ sit lower, between about 21% and 34%, though AI shows up in more than one in five merged pull requests in every language shown.

The repository data adds another angle. Among repositories created in 2026, TypeScript was the primary language in 35% of those with an observed agent signal, compared to 24% without one. For repositories created before 2026, the gap was similar: 27% with an agent signal, versus 17% without. That suggests developers who work with agents gravitate toward languages where agent output is easier to check. Developers who know exactly what they want still specify the language. But when they leave the choice open, agents appear to favor a narrower set of languages, TypeScript chief among them.

What is capturing developer attention

This year, we split the fastest-growing and most-engaged projects on GitHub into two groups: community and independent repositories, and single-vendor or product-led ones. Community and independent projects are foundation-governed, broadly maintained, or led by an individual without a clear commercial sponsor. Single-vendor and product-led projects are open source or source-available and often take substantial community contributions, but strategic control sits with one company.

Read together, the two lists show a division of labor. The community side is mostly the foundation underneath everything else: inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, frameworks like PyTorch, languages and runtimes like Rust and CPython, and platforms like Home Assistant and Godot. The vendor side is mostly the tools developers work with directly: coding agents, editors, and the orchestration around them. Contributors are showing up for both layers. The growth list also includes places built to welcome newcomers, like first-contributions and is-a-dev/register, where many developers make their first pull request.

This year’s fastest-growing repositories by contributors 
The most-engaged open-source repositories 

What doesn’t change

As part of our research this year, we also tracked the emoji developers used most in their repositories. Across every industry we looked at, the rocket 🚀 topped the list, by a wide margin. A fitting symbol for a year of momentum. Developers on GitHub covered more ground this year: more code, more countries, and more industries than we’ve ever measured. None of that activity changes who decides what the code should do. Someone still has to come up with the idea, whether it’s software that assesses earthquake risk, an open record of how online services change their terms and privacy policies, or an agent skill that makes an AI answer like a caveman to save on words. And someone still has to decide whether it works, whether it belongs, and whether it’s good.

What did change is how much easier it is to take an idea from a weekend thought to something real.

The tools will keep changing, and new industries will keep showing up in places we didn’t expect. What a developer chooses to build, and who they build it for, is still theirs to decide. Rocket emoji and all.

Glossary

  • Agent configuration file: A repository file that sets up or directs an AI coding agent. Also called an AI configuration file or agentic file. Repositories without one may still use AI.
  • Agent signal: An observed sign of agent involvement in telemetry, such as an agent-opened pull request. It is a floor, since not all agent use may be detected.
  • Agent-started pull request: A pull request whose first draft came from a coding agent that we can detect.
  • Auto model selection: A GitHub Copilot setting where Copilot picks the model for the task.
  • Commit: A saved snapshot of changes to a repository.
  • Contributions: Activity events: commenting on a commit, issue, pull request, or discussion; creating a gist, issue, pull request, or discussion; pushing code; and reviewing a pull request. Each push counts once, however many commits it holds. Open-source contributions are contributions to public and open source repositories.
  • Contributors: GitHub users with at least one contribution in the period.
  • Copilot cloud agent: A GitHub Copilot feature where a developer assigns a task and an agent works on it independently.
  • Dependabot: GitHub’s automated tool that finds outdated or vulnerable dependencies and opens pull requests to update them.
  • Developer-selected request: A model request where we proxied the developer chose the model. It excludes auto model selection, staff usage, duplicate monitoring and testing requests, background utility models, and requests made with a developer’s own API key.
  • GitHub Actions job: A single unit of work in a GitHub Actions workflow.
  • GitHub Advanced Security: GitHub’s suite of application security features, including code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review.
  • NAICS: The North American Industry Classification System, the standard sector taxonomy used this year to classify public repositories by industry.
  • Project HydraFusion: A GitHub research preview of model orchestration, which plans a task across models, such as one drafting, another reviewing, and a more capable one stepping in when needed. Now generally available as GitHub Copilot Fusion.
  • Push: Sending saved changes to GitHub. One push can carry many commits.
  • Stacked pull requests: A review workflow that splits related work into a sequence of smaller pull requests that are reviewed in order.

Methodology

  • Scope and window. The Octoverse year runs October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026, inclusive. Unless noted, metrics include public and private repositories. Industry, open-source contribution, and open-source project figures are public only. Prior years: 2024 and 2025 figures are recalculated on the same definitions and window, so they may differ from earlier reports, which covered public activity and a September 1 to August 31 window.
  • Pushes, commits, and contributions. A push sends one or more commits to GitHub. Contributions count each push once, so commit totals can exceed contribution totals. Actions are counted in jobs, not minutes. Open-source contributions (2.5 billion) are public.
  • Filtering. Contributor and contribution counts exclude spam-flagged accounts, staff, and bots where identifiable.
  • Geography and projections. Developers are mapped to countries by self-reported location, with a 100-developer publication threshold. Octoverse 2025 published 2030 totals, not annual targets. Progress is net developers added from September 2025 to September 2026 as a share of the distance from each country’s published 2025 count to its 2030 projection.
  • Languages. Contributors are distinct accounts each month that took part through pushes, pull requests, issues, reviews, or comments, attributed to each repository’s primary language (Linguist). An account can count in several languages. This follows the Octoverse 2025 method. Forecasts cover the top 10 languages by average monthly participation and project to September 2027 (mean shown).
  • The language bubble chart compares growth in monthly participating accounts between September 2025 and September 2026 with the share of merged pull requests with detected AI involvement. Bubble size reflects community size.
  • Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period, which were then used to construct ratios of ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes based on profile location vs. ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes based on IP address. These ratios were then used to weight the pushes from each country.
  • Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. AI mentions and agent-opened pull requests (detectable agents only) were flagged as separate signals. Sector and AI-mention shares can be related because both read the same text. Shares are estimates.
  • Open source rankings. We ranked public, non-fork repositories two ways. “Fastest-growing” ranks by the absolute year-over-year increase in distinct contributing accounts, not contribution counts. “Most engaged” blends a repository’s rankings for stars, forks, and distinct pull request and issue creators. We excluded forks, repositories whose activity reflects redistribution and results we identified as spam. Projects are grouped by governance: community and independent projects are foundation-hosted or independently run, and single-vendor projects follow one company’s product direction. Several community-hosted projects have commercial backers. The split describes governance and hosting, not funding or who employs maintainers.
  • Model choice. Figures cover GitHub Copilot and count developer-selected requests only. They exclude auto model selection, staff usage, duplicate monitoring requests, background utility models, and requests made with a developer’s own API key. Each model needs at least 1,000 weekly active users to count. Models are grouped by what they are built for, with examples listed alphabetically by provider:
  • Deep reasoning and planning: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 5.5.
  • General purpose: Claude Sonnet 5, Grok 4.7, GPT 6.1 Sol.
  • Fast and lightweight: Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT 6 Luna.
  • Figures describe observed use, not model quality. Trend observations use weekly data from July 14 to October 13, 2026.
  • Request share is the share of all qualifying requests per model group in a 7-day period ending October 13, 2026.
  • Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.
  • Forecasts. We ran 43 time-series and regression models on historical GitHub data, sign-ups, product usage, and market sizing, projecting developers on GitHub to September 2031 relative to September 2026. Outcomes group as 3x or more (21 models), 2x to under 3x (19), and under 2x (3). Octoverse 2025 used five models. No forecast is perfectly accurate.

Edited Nov. 6, 2026, to clarify the methodology language for open source rankings.

The post Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

entry.title: 开启AI码表时代？最贵骑行码表佳明1060评测
entry.content:
两年之约一到，佳明旗舰码表又更新了，两年前写时任旗舰1050时我说1050的更新乏善可陈，更像是1040 Plus。

1050虽然延续了佳明码表大而全的专业功能，但作为旗舰码表并没有太多独占的新功能，更多是UI和操作逻辑的优化，加上还有过重和码表架装不上的问题，在过去两年我依然沿用了1040。

而这次更新的Edge 1060，实实在在的有了旗舰码表的样子。

语音只是表象，AI码表才是未来

佳明1060的最大更新当然是语音功能，宣传片上一句“OK Garmin，开启骑行”收获了两极分化的评论，不是“酷毙了”就是“智商税拉完了”，实际真的如此吗？

高强度使用两周后我发现，这可能不仅仅是在骑行vlog里增加一个花絮的小功能，而又是一个“看起来智商税，实际真香”的功能。（咦，我为什么要说“又”）。

因为1060的语音功能并不是简单的语音功能——必须一字不差念准指令词的语音，而是支持一定的NLP自然语言处理，所以你不需要去记口令，你可以像用Siri控制iPhone那样控制1060，想让它做什么，直接和它对话就可以了。

因此宣传片上的那些”开启骑行“、“我的最大速度是多少”只是最基础的功能，你完全可以用它干更多的事：

在电梯里直接用语音命令让它规划一条导航路线；

又或者在骑车时觉得耳机音乐声有点小时让它把声音调大一点；

还有在铁三比赛换项手忙脚乱没空开启码表的时候喊一声；

再或者在骑车去集合点快要迟到时给同伴发一条语音信息……要我说，佳明早该做这个功能了，一方面语音在骑行这种双手不便的场景里天然好用，

另一方面，佳明码表的功能实在太多太全，很多设置藏得很深，与其让用户翻菜单，不如直接开口告诉它你要什么，这跟如今手机厂商用AI助手接管操作的思路如出一辙。

目前来说，语音的实际使用效果大概有一半的成功率，理解能力不能算很强，大概就是弱化版的初生Siri和小爱同学的水平，没有完整大模型的语音终究不能指望太多，也许可以考虑学苹果AI把简单指令放本地，复杂放云端的思路，简单指令码表搞定，复杂指令调用手机算力？

另外也受环境影响，室内安静环境的成功率是很高的，骑起来之后比较随机，我有过在高速下坡中成功唤醒的经历，也有过安静爬坡时失败的经历。

佳明就该做个运动耳机，顺便把手表上的音乐功能下放到码表上，既能听音乐又能当做语音控制的入口，还能结合GroupRide功能当做骑行对讲机用，多好。

在语音管用的时候，确实好用，就像我已经习惯了让小爱同学给我开关灯/窗帘/空调一样，我现在也开始习惯用语音进行很多码表操作了。

目前我最常用的功能是校准功率计，作为一个功率计爱好者，每次做功率计测评光是校准都要点击好几步，现在一个语音就搞定了，简单多了。

另外还有一些不常用偶尔又想知道的数据直接用语音用也很方便，比如在骑某个路线时问它骑完大概几点，在山顶聊天时问它一句现在海拔是多少。

还有那天骑完回家手机没电关机，又恰逢长安街管制需要绕道，虽然带了两码表，但另一个没了手机就没法用，直接用语音让1060给我规划了一条回家路线，不用在码表上点来点去的。

而且在我看来，语音只是个表象，就像AI手机里语音只是一个入口一样，在未来只是个让码表直接得到结果的方式，考虑到最近佳明刚好在1060发布同期开放了个人API接口，可以接入AI大模型中，不免让人多想。

也许要不了多久我们的骑行可能是这样的：微信群里收到了一个有些意思的路线或者赛段，直接转发给AI助手直接让码表生成一个合适的路线，还顺带再用“功率指导”功能生成一个骑行指导，路上还会根据你的“实时体力”和天气状况给你进行“智能补给”提醒。

如果是未来计划，码表还可以根据你的状态让“Garmin教练”给你“每日训练建议”，帮助你更好的骑下来。路上开启“GroupRide”能看到相互位置，互相发短信/语音，如果有意外“侦测事故”码表自行紧急联系。

这些都是佳明码表已经有的功能，只需要将它们打通就有无限玩法，1060的语音功能只是一个开始。除了语音，还有一些小进步除了语音控制这个重要更新，1060也更新了一些新功能，有好有坏。

更高效的UI界面

1060大改了赛段、训练和爬坡规划这三个最重要的骑行功能UI，让LCD触摸屏发挥了更大的作用，以往这几个界面是写死的，设置好就无法调整，1060让它们都动起来了。

如今在这几个界面里，可以通过上下滑动改变不同元素的位置，比如赛段和爬坡规划中，下拉能让地图区域更大，上拉则能展开海拔图，看清自己与PB/KOM的相对位置。

在训练界面上下拉可以在全程训练、当前阶段等多个信息中切换，也是很方便。

更好的硬件设计

在我用过的众多佳明码表中，1060的硬件设计无疑是最好的，尤其是在前代1050诸多bug的映衬下。

不仅大幅缩减了长度解决了1050部分码表架装不上的问题，也终于给到了840之后就一直期待的实体按键，而且屏幕素质也有了提升，对比度更高色彩更舒服了，似乎电子铃铛的声音也变大了一点，续航还有一点反向虚标略微增长，开着导航、连着功率和心率骑了7小时，只掉了30%的电。

应急救命的反向充电

佳明1060如今不仅可以用手机给它充电，还能用码表给手机充电，这个功能是不错的，尤其是对我们这些老旧小电池iPhone用户来说，只是我测试下来1060的电池不太够iPhone霍霍的，没有快充，半小时给iPhone 15Pro充了33%，但是1060的电量消耗了72%。

虽然结合前面的1060骑行耗电量看，理论上来说满电出门可以让你骑个六七小时后还能给手机充个30%的电让你没电的iPhone续一下命打个货拉拉回家，但你得记着在车上藏一根充电线。

更简单的团骑模式

GroupRide绝对是佳明最被低估的功能，这个功能值得俱乐部大力推广，不仅方便领骑管理，也能让大家骑行中有更多好玩的功能，还可以避免有人走丢甚至出意外。

几年前环台湾骑行时，当时的地接导游就让我们在手机上装了个APP来实时定位防止走丢，那APP在国区还没上架，好一番折腾，当时要有这个功能那就方便多了。

之前的GroupRide在设置好之后需要发送一个链接点击添加或者是输入一个6位数的进群码才能用，而现在只需离的够近就能看到附近开启的GroupRide，就可以申请进群了。

进群之后就可以共享骑行路线，互相看到位置距离、实时的速度功率和心率了，还能互相发信息，爬完坡也有排行榜和徽章奖励，挺有意思的。

其他还有一些小改进也不错，比如可以设置替代数据，依靠传感器的数据栏可以加一个备选，比如换到没有功率计的小布上就可以把功率数据自动替换成当前时间什么的。

再比如通知中心里有了细分APP可选，这些小更新有点意思，但不多，就不展开了。接下来我们聊聊一些没那么好的更新和不好的改变。

门槛降低依然有点高的骑行导航

首先，我们需要明确一下码表导航的概念到底是什么，再基于这个前提谈好用与否。

码表导航的逻辑和手机导航是不一样的，手机导航是“找地方”，码表导航是“找路线”——前者只要到得了，后者必须骑得爽。

手机是我要去哪，看看怎么去，可以走三环也可以走四环，无所谓，能到就行。

码表是我要骑什么路线，爬哪个坡，跟着走这个路线，即使是要去哪个地方，那也是要设计路线，需把途中的坡规划进去，是绕不开的。

高德百度给的路线不一定适合骑行，所以要规划一条路线，那自然是不存在“改地点”这个情况，如果是那个路线临时骑不了，那就是换整个路线，所以是重新选路线或者手机下发路线。

最佳骑行路线一定是在Strava/Komoot这样的路线社区上找到热门的路线/赛段然后将它们串起来，而不是简单的导航。

延展阅读

 

在佳明上，其实是两个都有，路线导航就是我们通常在Komoot/Strava上画好路线或者导入现成的GPX跟着走。

佳明还有一个叫“路径导航”，佳明路线导航和路径导航都是可以设置走错路是重新规划还是回到原路线的，只是设置藏得非常深，这就又回到了语音控制那个话题了。

1060的路径导航其实增加了许多新功能，比如在规划路线时，有多条路线选择，就像你用高德导航会给你不同时间的路线一样，不同的路线爬升和时间都有标注。

另外它还会结合“路况信息”中新增的“封路”信息以及大数据中骑行数据规划一条“停顿少、交叉路口少且不易减速拥堵的畅行训练路线”，但就我常骑的地点规划出来的看并不尽如人意，我还是更倾向于走大路、走直线少拐弯的策略来规划路线，除非是手机没电这种极端情况，我还是更喜欢掏出手机在Komoot上花几分钟画一条路线同步过来。

不过1060新增加了一个兴趣点功能倒是还不错，可以看到附近的厕所、便利店这些，有种玩游戏探索地图的意思，实测在城里临时找个厕所确实很方便。

违背祖训的菜单设计

1060上我最不喜欢的改变是下拉菜单，就像是Mac OS 26改掉了启动台一样，佳明把下拉菜单中的许多功能整合在了一个集合页里，完全破坏了多年使用的肌肉记忆，经常想找个设置找不到，啊，好像又回到语音控制的环节了。

另外整合后许多功能缩在一起并不好选择，我不止一次的误触了背光控制，在看不清和眼瞎之间徘徊。

还有所谓的“骑行前准备清单”，将每个活动模式的设置整合到一起了，美其名曰骑行前检查一下，但更好的不是应该设置好一次之后就不动了吗，像多个传感器直接固定分配给不同活动模式不就好了，还需要我每次骑之前查看用了哪些传感器吗？原本可以在下拉菜单很轻松进入活动模式的设置，现在得多按好几次按钮才能找到。

原地踏步的骑行训练功能

Garmin教练是个不错的训练功能，它的用法和课程设置和我之前每年一千多买的TrainerRoad几乎一模一样，你用它练到4瓦是肯定没问题的。但考虑到佳明在今年刚收购了全球最大的训练平台TrainingPeaks与TrainHeroic，我对1060有期待的，结果1060的训练功能只是更新了“仅心率带”训练，将训练功能下探到了没有功率计的用户，我就……

只能说大概还需要时间吧，考虑到我四年前的1040还在OTA新功能，相信无论是明年随着560/860一起更新，还是得下一代的1070，现在买1060应该都能享用到，亏不了。

总结

我一直的观点都是，买东西不仅要看它的长板够不够长，突出的优点是否够吸引你，更要看它的短板有多短，缺点是否会抹杀掉那些优点。目前看，佳明1060的确是目前最好的码表，它延续了佳明40系以来所有的优点，在我用过的所有高端码表里唯一没有硬伤，且功能最丰富的，除了贵点没毛病，许多的独占功能和最大优势IQ插件可以看这两篇。

为何码表分佳明和其他，这些独占功能可能就是底气

Connect IQ 插件有多强？佳明用户必看的功能扩展指北

1060在这个基础上又增加了一些可圈可点的小改进和语音控制这个大更新，让一些功能和设置都更好用了，你不必再记住每条设置藏在第几层菜单，或者某某功能怎么开启，在1060上只要开口就行。

它有一些短板和不足，一部分像自由爬坡规划不准这些都可以通过换地图解决（点击阅读原文有方案，提取码a1mb），另一部分属于是闹心但可以忍。

对于绝大多数人来说，1060肯定是太贵了，你也不需要花那么多钱买它，语音好用是未来但在当下不是骑行必需，佳明有一点好，和iPhone一样，核心骑行功能从低端到高端几乎是一样的，差别更多是屏幕和一些硬件限制的功能，很多1060的新功能也会OTA给50系乃至40系。

佳明全套骑行生态的门槛其实只有一千多点，540除了按键操控有点繁琐但功能是齐全的，所有你需要的数据、进阶骑行、路线规划、训练指导、状态分析、教练功能、趣味功能都有。

在我这目前综合最佳是840，按键触控双行，真正的全能，价格还实惠。如果对屏幕色彩和外放喇叭有需求就选择550或者850。

对于那些喜欢旗舰产品，体验最新技术的人当然还是1060，六千多的价格对于它的用户群来说也还好，两年置换一块码表再怎么也比年年换新iPhone和各种年更新势力便宜，只要它的确是最强码表就行。

开启AI码表时代？最贵骑行码表佳明1060评测https://sspai.com/post/118615

entry.title: 国产化率100%！首款鸿蒙台式机亮相 华为从芯片到系统的全栈自主可控
entry.content:
快科技11月5日消息，今天下午鸿蒙办公产业峰会将在武汉正式召开，不少消费者期待多时的首款鸿蒙台式机产品也将和公众见面。

这款命名为擎云HM650的机型此前已经在华为官方网站上做过展示，从11月5日开始将面向全市场正式大规模上市发售，产品主打政企、金融、能源等各类商用场景，核心目标是实现全链路从芯片到操作系统的全栈自主可控。

此前在2026华为全联接大会上，华为就已经首次公开展示了这款首款预装自研鸿蒙操作系统的台式电脑擎云HM650。

随着这款台式机的落地，华为鸿蒙电脑产品线已经集齐了笔记本、折叠屏、台式机三类核心形态，整套产品从底层芯片到上层操作系统全部是华为全栈自研，正式摆脱了桌面领域长期对Windows、Linux两大海外系统生态的依赖。

从公开的硬件配置来看，这款机型搭载华为自研的麒麟X90处理器，采用10核20线程架构，集成Maliang 910 GPU，搭配华为专属创新双层散热架构。

依托软件、硬件、芯片、云端的深度协同机制，可以长时间持续输出高性能算力，既可以满足日常普通综合办公的需求，也能支撑工程设计、仿真建模、软件编程这类对算力要求较高的专业场景使用。

麒麟X90芯片和配套搭载的鸿蒙专业版操作系统，双双通过了安全可靠II级认证，因此这款机型的核心服务群体定向面向政企、金融这类对信息安全等级要求极高的场景，还特意针对企业和政务客户的不同使用需求拆分出了两个专属版本。

最值得行业关注的是，这款首款鸿蒙台式机已经实现了全部元器件国产率100%，是国内首款完全不依赖海外供应链部件的商用整机产品。

entry.title: Agents Aren’t Humans (But They Kinda Are)
entry.content:
AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action?

“Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits.

Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries. An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. 

This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents").

This post rests on one principle:

The Intermediation Principle: The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation.

A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign.

The intermediary problem

Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd.

The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business.

Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra.

Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra.

None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today.

A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents.

In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost. That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved.

Our vision

Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification.

None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action. It requires that Sites have the means to obtain or require information about the User to hold them accountable, when applicable, with or without an Agent.

What people have tried, and why they fall short

A common proposal is for Agents to pass a Site's CAPTCHA through to the User to solve. That proves some human is present at that moment (“human in the loop”, or HITL), and nothing more. HITL is primarily a mechanism to prevent mistakes from misalignment. Misalignment is an issue between the Operator and the User, and resolving it does not resolve the majority of the problems above. For example, it can't tell Bob from anyone else (Traffic commingling), and it says nothing about who the Agent acts for the rest of the time. Additionally, Agents exist to remove friction, and HITL adds back that friction, so Operators are incentivized to remove or bypass it for the User.

Another common proposal is to use tightly scoped access controls. Agents are built to do anything a User could, so in practice they ask for, and get, permission to do everything. A scope of "everything" tells the Site nothing. And even a narrow scope only says what the Agent was allowed to do. It doesn't say who answers when the Agent gets it wrong, which is the question the Site actually needs answered.

What the web needs

The web needs tools and protocols that allow Sites and Agents to collaborate to determine what behaviors and actions are allowed, as well as express preferences and policies from Sites to Agents, all in a way that can be reasonably supported by all Sites and Agents. Fortunately, work is already underway along all of these fronts, and many, if not all, of these can be addressed by applying existing standards.

Protocols

Agents and Sites can engage in explicit protocols for solving some of the problems above. For instance, MOLE is one upcoming approach that aims for rate limiting without User-specific identifiers, allowing Sites to transition away from implicit identities and towards explicit protocols for accomplishing the same goal. This is similar to the x402 protocol, which aims to enable payments on the web while remaining privacy-preserving. We are actively exploring ways in which we can leverage existing protocols for addressing other problems, as well as exploring designing new protocols when existing solutions fall short.

Identities

When discussing Agent Identity, Web Bot Auth (WBA) is our preferred method. WBA allows an Agent to sign its requests, which provides a secure way for an Agent to identify itself (and, implicitly, the Operator). We must still define a mechanism that supports multiple intermediaries: when Agent A uses Agent B inside Browser C, the Site needs to be able to know this, so that the Site can correctly ensure that access by Agent A is correctly understood and controlled, for example, in order to prevent Policy circumvention.

Other types of identifying information, such as session, account, or even User-specific IDs, might be necessary, depending on the context. We are working with the relevant standards to explore ways to communicate such identifying information.

Let’s take a look into types of Identity in regards to a User. Ultimately, Identity is a spectrum that trades various degrees of information about a user, while ideally practicing principles of data minimization. Identity provides us a mechanism to answer “who are you?” in pursuit of answering the follow-up questions of: “are you who you say you are?” and “can we trust you?”.

In many cases, identifying information isn’t needed, and privacy-preserving methods for moderating access to agents, such as through Privacy Pass and MOLE, can help us answer “can we trust you?” without needing to answer “who are you?”. Private Access Tokens was one early way in which we tried to establish trust without identifying the user, and MOLE is intended to be the successor to this technology. However, there are cases where graduated forms of disclosure along this spectrum would be needed, and you can generally characterize them in the following ways:

  1. Nothing - Users may act on the internet while bringing no identifiers to the table.
  2. Session - Sites require some way of linking requests in the same session to a single agent. This allows the Site to establish reputation for a given session and act on it accordingly. For example, Poppy has a notion of a session ID for exactly this purpose. 
  3. Account - Sites require a way of attributing requests to the same User across sessions. This might be a stable identifier assigned by an Operator or third party to a User that persists across the account with the Operator, such as a single Agent visiting the same Site every day using the same identifier. An example use case this would enable is: “Bind your Site account to your Agent account”.
  4. Unique - Some Sites might require a unique, per-User identifier provisioned by a third party that persists across Operators, accounts, Agents, and sessions. This may be useful for high risk actions, or for Sites that need to provide limited access to an expensive resource or that have very restrictive obligations or compliance requirements. Government IDs, third party identity verification, and decentralized technologies like Proof of Human are all examples of technologies that can provide this.

Ultimately, Sites determine what information they need for clients to answer “is the entity behind this request allowed to do this action at this time?” In many cases, protocols already exist, or are being developed, to convey this information: WBA for conveying an Agent’s platform identity, MOLE for conveying User reputation, OAuth for conveying account identities, and so on.

Claims

Beyond identities, some actions require a fact about the real person, such as being over 18 or being the cardholder (Identity verification breaks, Friendly fraud). Often the Operator verified this at sign-up or a third party already has this information. 

In order to allow Agents access to Sites or actions with these kinds of restrictions, we need mechanisms for Sites to request this information, and for Operators or third parties to provide this information.

Site Agent access policy

Today, an Agent infers a Site’s rules by trying something and interpreting the Site response (usually, whether it gets blocked). That wastes resources on both sides, and in some cases makes honest Agents appear to be malicious. Robots.txt says where a crawler may go, but isn’t fully suited to express what Agents may do.

Sites need a machine-readable way to publish what actions Agents are allowed to do. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is actively working on some preference expression mechanisms for this, primarily in the AI Preferences Working Group. However, the focus of the group is on expressing preferences for use (such as training, inference, and search), and there is still not a group focused on the larger need for preference expression mechanisms discussed here.

On open source and local Agents

Agents that are not run as an “Intermediary” (e.g. on-device Agents, or locally hosted Agents such as OpenClaw) raise different concerns. Primarily, they look like (and are) automation, and they have no single party to build reputation or hold accountability with.

There are many solutions to this, one of which is to ask these Agents to provide a Unique ID. However, addressing this is not the initial focus of Trusted Agent Delegation.

What’s next

Real-world solutions to the problems that Sites face won’t emerge from fragmented, vendor-specific mechanisms. They require open, interoperable standards that are rooted in real world experience. We have been, and continue to actively collaborate across the ecosystem, with major Operators, identity verification companies, payment providers, merchants, publishers, proxy providers, and cloud browsing companies, to align operational requirements directly with active work on these problems in the IETF and elsewhere 

Our focus is on bridging the gap between running code and emerging specifications across working groups and activities like Web Bot Auth, AIPREFs, OAuth, WIMSE, and MOLE. We are doing this, in part, by co-authoring and refining open protocols like WBA and MOLE and building and deploying implementations of these protocols at scale.

We are also announcing the Trusted Agent Delegation (TAD) coalition. The goal of TAD is to bring a group of representatives across the ecosystem to have discussions on the overall problem set that was put forth in this document, examine all existing protocols, and then to bring more well-defined problems or problems to the IETF to work through, as needed. We intend to hold side meetings at the IETF and workshops in the future to facilitate discussion.

If you are building agents, agent runtimes, running an edge or cloud platform, or managing commercial or compliance applications or infrastructure, we need you to get involved in these efforts too. Check out this page for more information on how to participate.

What you can do today

An open, interoperable foundation  is where we're headed, starting with TAD. But you don't have to wait for new protocols to start regaining visibility and control. As of this week, Cloudflare customers can take three concrete steps:

See which Agents are on your site, and what they're doing. Security Analytics now breaks out Personal Assistants as their own traffic category, and a new widget lists every Agent visiting your site, how many requests each one sends, the paths it hits, and the errors it runs into. Unexplained automated traffic becomes traffic you can reason about. And for the broader picture of AI crawlers and bots affect your business, including how much each Operator crawls versus the traffic it sends back, Enterprise Bot Management customers can use Business Insights.

Set access on your terms, per Agent. Using AI Crawler and Agent access policies, you can welcome the Agents that bring you business and restrict the ones that don't — allow an Agent across your site, block it only on pages with ads, or block it entirely. Your Search and Training policies stay independent.

Tie an Agent back to the user it acts for — and act on it. For sites using Account Abuse Protection (early access), every login and sign-up now shows whether a personal Agent made the request, and which one. When an attacker abuses a shared Agent on one account, you can mitigate that account — with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID — without blocking the Agent for every other legitimate user behind it. This is a first, concrete answer to the Traffic commingling challenge described above: you can finally see past the Agent to the User, and respond accordingly.

These are the first building blocks of the vision, already in production. More will follow as the standards mature.

And if your company has a more restrictive position on Agents, we would love to hear it. Reach out and share your problems with us directly. We are looking to help build an Internet where site owners have visibility and control, but also where Agents have the maximum access that is reasonable within those controls. You can reach out to your Customer Support team, or email us at crawlercontrols@cloudflare.com.

Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)https://blog.cloudflare.com/trusted-agent-delegation/

entry.title: 今年是华为进入PC产业第10年！鸿蒙电脑达成全新里程碑：发货量破百万
entry.content:
快科技11月5日消息，华为董事、终端BG CEO何刚表示，鸿蒙电脑发货量已突破100万台。从华为MateBook Fold非凡大师的折叠创新，到华为MateBook Pro S 798g的轻薄体验，这一成绩离不开每一位用户、产业链伙伴和开发者的支持。

今年也是华为进入PC产业的第十年，目前鸿蒙电脑应用已经超过2.1万个，覆盖学习办公、AI生产力、专业设计以及休闲娱乐等多个场景，能够满足越来越多用户的日常需求。

众所周知，传统PC、平板和手机往往拥有相对独立的使用环境。用户在不同设备之间切换时，经常需要重新寻找文件、传输资料，操作链路较为繁琐。

比如在平板上查阅会议材料，回到工位后还要用电脑修改文件，中间往往需要经过发送、下载、另存等多个步骤。如果内容可以跨设备流转、任务能够接续，用户就能少做一次传输，也少花时间确认手头的是哪个版本。

鸿蒙操作系统正是针对这一痛点，通过打通手机、平板和电脑之间的设备壁垒，让用户可以更加便捷地实现文件流转、任务接续和多设备协作，进一步提升办公效率。设备之间的协同不再只是简单的文件互传，而是让任务和内容在不同终端之间自然衔接。

随着移动办公和多终端协作成为常态，设备之间的协同效率也成为影响体验的重要因素之一。鸿蒙通过系统级能力打通多设备体验，为未来全场景办公提供了新的发展方向，也让办公场景中的设备切换更加顺畅。
